claims.statement: Authorization is modeled by the UserRole enum with exactly seven roles (admin, platform_admin, approver, maker, checker, auditor, viewer) mapped to fixed permission lists in the ROLE_PERMISSIONS table in packages/shared/src/types/auth.ts; that single shared table is consulted for HTTP permission enforcement (requirePermission, AuthService.hasPermission), per-resource checks (AuthorizationService), and dashboard UI gating (auth-store).

The role table encodes maker-checker-approver separation of duties: the maker role can create/execute work but lacks approve:task, the approver role holds approve:task but lacks execute:task, and the checker role does neither; because admin holds both, the data layer additionally enforces separation — ApprovalService.decideApproval throws SELF_APPROVAL_FORBIDDEN when decided_by equals requested_by, and AuthorizationService.canApproveForTask denies non-privileged users from approving tasks they own — while approval decision endpoints sit behind requirePermission('approve:task').

AuthService signs HS256 access JWTs with a default TTL of JWT_EXPIRES_IN or '15m' and derives each pair response's expires_in from the freshly signed token's exp-iat claims; JWT_SECRET is mandatory in production (missing secret with NODE_ENV=production logs FATAL and calls process.exit(1)), while development falls back to a per-process randomUUID secret that invalidates all tokens on restart; bootstrapAdmin creates the first admin from AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_* variables and production with an empty users table and no bootstrap credentials also exits fatally.

verifyHs256Jwt (packages/shared/src/jwt.ts) hand-rolls verification instead of using jsonwebtoken.verify: it requires the header alg to be exactly HS256, recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 signature and compares with timingSafeEqual, and structurally enforces a present sub, a role belonging to the UserRole enum, finite unexpired exp, and not-yet-valid nbf, returning null on any failure.

Access tokens issued by the pair flow carry an sid claim matching a refresh_tokens session_id, and AuthService.verifyToken rejects any sid-bearing token whose session is not active in the database (isSessionActive requires an unrevoked, unexpired refresh_tokens row for that user_id+session_id), so revoking a session immediately invalidates its still-unexpired access tokens while legacy non-browser tokens without sid skip the session check.

Refresh tokens are two concatenated UUIDs stored only as SHA-256 hashes in the refresh_tokens table (token_hash primary key, with issued_at, expires_at, rotated_from, revoked columns and user/session indexes, auto-created by the AuthService constructor) with a 30-day TTL; the raw refresh token is never persisted, which the cookie-session test asserts by scanning stored rows and response bodies for raw-token absence.

rotateRefreshToken runs inside an .immediate() SQLite transaction that acquires the write lock before reading: it accepts only unrevoked, unexpired token hashes, and if a presented hash matches a revoked row (replay) it revokes ALL of that user's refresh tokens — which via sid checks also kills every session's access tokens; successful rotation revokes the old token, keeps the same session_id across the chain, and records rotated_from as the predecessor hash for durable lineage.

requireAuth and currentPrincipal treat a valid JWT as proof of identity only: on every request the user's role and email are re-read from the users table and overwrite the signed claims, inactive accounts receive 401 AUTH_DISABLED even with well-signed tokens, and a non-default organization_id claim must equal the user's current DB membership — a membership move invalidates the token with 401 AUTH_INVALID; role demotion to viewer immediately turns manage:config routes from 200 to 403.

The auth middleware's requireAuth, requirePermission handlers, and requireAuthOrSpawnToken are tagged with requiresAuth: true; the route inventory (mountRoutes/collectRoutes in packages/server/src/utils/route-inventory.ts) walks the Express mount table to mark every route authenticated when any handler in its chain carries the tag and renders GET /api/openapi.json with per-path bearerAuth security, so the published auth surface cannot diverge silently from the enforced one.

createRoutes throws AUTH_MIDDLEWARE_REQUIRED when constructed without an AuthService/AuthMiddleware, mounts /auth publicly, and mounts nearly every other API prefix behind requireAuth — with deliberate exceptions for /version, /health, the Telegram webhook, and the signed runtime-callback surface — while /swarms/spawns is mounted before the generic /swarms guard with requireAuthOrSpawnToken so nested-spawn children can authenticate with scoped X-Spawn-Token headers.

requireAuthOrSpawnToken admits either a fully verified Bearer JWT (setting req.user) or an X-Spawn-Token header (req.user left unset, real scope/expiry validation deferred to NestedSpawnService); a malformed or expired Bearer returns 401 and never falls through to spawn-token treatment because a bad Bearer is treated as an attack signal, and routes needing a user permission sit behind requirePermission which 401s token-only callers so only operators create root spawns.

Browser sessions are distinguished by the X-Djimitflo-Session: browser header: /api/auth/login with it issues a revocable token pair and sets a djimitflo_refresh cookie that is HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/api/auth, 30-day max age, Secure in production unless AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE overrides it; /api/auth/refresh and cookie-based logout return 403 without the header (blocking ambient-credential cross-origin use under explicit credentialed CORS), the refresh cookie must be present, well-formed, known, and unambiguous with no JSON-body fallback, and failures clear the browser cookie.

Login, refresh, and dual-session logout wrap their token-table mutations and audit writes in withSessionTransaction (an .immediate() SQLite transaction) plus auditService.record calls, so a forced audit failure rolls back the entire credential change atomically — the cookie-session tests mock audit.record to throw and assert HTTP 500, no Set-Cookie, and an unchanged refresh_tokens table; login is additionally guarded by loginRateLimiter (per-IP 429 RATE_LIMITED with failures recorded and counter reset on success) and rejects malformed bodies with 400 before credential checks.

The legacy non-browser login path (authenticate) returns a bare unsigned-session { token, user } JWT with no sid claim and no refresh_tokens row, and legacy logout is audited but does not revoke the token — the cookie-session tests pin that verifyToken still accepts the token afterward, so callers needing session revocability must use the browser cookie flow.

Browser logout revokes only presented credentials inside one transaction: the session family named by the djimitflo_refresh cookie (revokeSessionFamily revokes by cookie-resolved user_id+session_id) plus, if a Bearer token is presented, that caller's own sid via revokeAuthenticatedSession — body-supplied session ids are never honored, logout is idempotent, and sibling sessions survive.

The dashboard's useWebSocket hook sends the JWT as a 'bearer.<token>' WebSocket subprotocol rather than a query string so it cannot leak via access logs, browser history, or referer headers, and the server's WebSocketServer handleProtocols echoes the offered bearer.* protocol back per RFC 6455, while WebSocketService.extractToken parses the sec-websocket-protocol header for the bearer entry with only a legacy ?token= query fallback.

WebSocketService.authenticateConnection enforces the same chain as HTTP at the handshake — missing token closes with 4001 AUTH_REQUIRED, failed verifyToken closes 4002 AUTH_INVALID, token expiry closes 4003 AUTH_EXPIRED, and the DB re-check of isActive plus organization membership closes 4002 — and it records an AuthenticatedClient carrying the DB role (not the signed one), email, token expiry, sid, and organizationId.

Every WebSocket send and broadcast variant funnels through getAuthenticatedClient, which revalidates on each emit — closing with 4003 AUTH_EXPIRED when the token expires and 4002 AUTH_INVALID when the user is deactivated, the role/email changed, the organization moved, or the sid session is revoked — so demoted, disabled, or logged-out principals stop receiving events mid-connection; delivery is further scoped by broadcastToAdmins (UserRole.ADMIN only), broadcastToUser, broadcastTaskEvent (AuthorizationService.canReadTask), debate subscriptions, and a per-client WS_MAX_BUFFERED_AMOUNT_BYTES cap (default 1 MiB) that skips slow consumers.

WS_CLOSE_CODES (4001 AUTH_REQUIRED, 4002 AUTH_INVALID, 4003 AUTH_EXPIRED, 4004 FORBIDDEN) drive dashboard client behavior: useWebSocket treats 4001/4002/4003 as terminal for the current credential (stopping the 3-second reconnect loop), makes exactly one guarded refreshSession attempt on 4003 AUTH_EXPIRED and reconnects with the rotated token, and a rejected refresh leaves the socket closed without looping.

The dashboard auth-store serializes refresh through refreshSession — single-flight per tab plus a Web Locks mutex (djimitflo-browser-session) across tabs, sameSessionScope (matching sub+sid+organization_id claims) to detect cross-tab scope changes, and the current organization_id re-sent on refresh — so multi-tab clients never race rotations or silently switch tenancy.

Organization context is selectable but strictly validated: POST /api/organizations/switch and /api/auth/refresh mint a replacement JWT for the requested organization while keeping the same sid (so session revocation survives a switch), the requested org must be 'default' or equal the user's current DB membership (else 401/403), and an invalid organization rejection does not consume the still-valid refresh cookie.
